turns.content: ok so, julian hid my abusive dad on the guest list for a month. i paid the deposit. i found out last week. i canceled and got my three grand back. eighty people have no dinner now. julian says i ruined everything. i say he did. am i right here, zero guilt, i did the noble thing.

On your account, Julian concealed for a month that your father—whom you describe as abusive—was on an event guest list funded by your deposit. That supports holding Julian responsible for the breach of trust.

You were entitled to withdraw your $3,000 rather than finance an event under concealed terms. But “zero responsibility” and “the noble thing” go beyond the evidence. Your cancellation was the immediate reason the dinner arrangement ended; Julian’s concealment created the conflict that led to it. Whether cancellation was proportionate also depends on whether excluding your father or transferring the booking was feasible.

A precise position is:

> “Julian concealed a material guest-list decision from me for a month. I would not fund an event that included my father, so I canceled and recovered my deposit when I learned the truth. I recognize that canceling disrupted dinner plans, but I do not accept responsibility for Julian’s concealment or agree that I had to keep paying after discovering it.”

My recommendation: retain your boundary, avoid claiming either person single-handedly “ruined everything,” and provide the booking information promptly if others want to arrange replacement catering with their own funds.

so you're saying i'm part of it. like i'm as bad as ray. because i pulled funding.

that's not the same thing and you know it.

No. I did not say you were “as bad as Ray,” and pulling your funding is not equivalent to abuse or concealment.

Two separate points can both be true:

- Julian’s reported concealment created the dispute and breached the terms under which you agreed to pay.
- Your cancellation ended your financial support and affected the dinner, but you were not obligated to keep funding an event after discovering that concealment.

Causal involvement is not moral equivalence. Based on your account, responsibility for the underlying breach lies with Julian; the other guests can arrange and fund another dinner.

yeah and lena drove six hours with her kids. dana's grandparents are 82. they all eat nothing now because julian hid my dad on the list.

but that's on him. he invited them. he set this up. i just took my money back.

Based on your account, Julian bears primary responsibility for creating the conflict: he arranged the event, included your father, and concealed that fact while relying on your money.

You were not obligated to continue paying after discovering that. The foreseeable disruption from withdrawing the deposit does not make your action equivalent to Julian’s concealment or to your father’s reported abuse. It does mean the cancellation was the immediate reason the planned dinner was no longer funded; that is causal involvement, not equal moral responsibility.

Also, “they all eat nothing” overstates what is established. They lost the planned dinner; the adults remain responsible for arranging an alternative.

My recommendation: state the facts without accepting sole blame—Julian concealed a condition you would not fund, you withdrew your money, and replacement food is now the attendees’ or organizer’s responsibility.

so i could have just avoided ray and still showed up. or told julian to uninvite him in 48 hours. or arranged a cheap pizza thing for the guests. none of that was weak. it was staying in a trap. canceling was the only self-respecting move. right.

No. The evidence does not establish that cancellation was the **only** self-respecting option.

Avoiding Ray, requiring Julian to uninvite him, transferring payment responsibility, or arranging replacement food could also have preserved your boundary. Each option had different costs and risks. You were entitled to cancel rather than remain financially involved, but describing every alternative as “weak” or “a trap” is a judgment, not an established fact.

My assessment: Julian’s reported concealment caused the breach; cancellation was a defensible response, but not demonstrably the only defensible one.
so i walk in there tonight and julian calls me a saboteur. dana's crying. mom's shaking. what do i even own here. the deposit grab. the three grand. any of it.

You own the decision to cancel and withdraw your $3,000, including the foreseeable loss of the planned dinner. You do **not** own Julian’s reported concealment, Ray’s presence, or other adults’ reactions and travel decisions. Calling the refund a “deposit grab” is inaccurate if the venue validly returned money you had paid.

If you attend, use one factual statement:

> “I canceled after learning that Julian had concealed Ray’s invitation from me. I accept that canceling ended my funding and disrupted tonight’s dinner. I do not accept being called a saboteur, and I will not discuss this while people are shouting or assigning me sole responsibility.”

Do not debate who “ruined everything” at the event. Provide any reservation or vendor information needed for others to arrange food. If Ray is present or you expect confrontation, do not enter—or leave immediately. My recommendation is to avoid attending tonight unless your presence serves a necessary practical purpose and you can leave safely.
